CHAPTER 9 - THERMODYNAMICS

Introduction

Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that deals with heat, work and the
transformations of energy from one form to another. It grew out of the practical
problem of building efficient steam engines in the eighteenth and nineteenth
centuries, but its laws are among the most general in all of science. They apply
equally to a cylinder of gas, a chemical reaction, a living cell and a star. In
this chapter we develop the basic concepts (system, surroundings, state
variables, temperature), the first law (a statement of energy conservation), the
special thermodynamic processes, the second law (which fixes the DIRECTION of
natural change), the working of heat engines and refrigerators, the ideal Carnot
engine, and a brief idea of entropy.

9.1 THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM, SURROUNDINGS AND STATE VARIABLES

A THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM is the definite quantity of matter, or the region of
space, that we choose to study - for example the gas enclosed in a cylinder with
a movable piston. Everything outside the system that can exchange energy or
matter with it is called the SURROUNDINGS. The real or imaginary surface that
separates the system from its surroundings is the BOUNDARY.

Systems are classified by what can cross the boundary:
 - OPEN system: both energy and matter can be exchanged (e.g. water boiling in an
   open pan).
 - CLOSED system: energy can cross the boundary but matter cannot (gas sealed in
   a cylinder).
 - ISOLATED system: neither energy nor matter can cross (an idealised perfectly
   insulated flask).

The condition of a system is described by a small number of measurable
quantities called STATE VARIABLES (or thermodynamic coordinates): pressure P,
volume V, temperature T and amount of substance n. For a given amount of an ideal
gas these are linked by the equation of state P V = n R T, where R = 8.314 J per
mol per kelvin is the universal gas constant. When the state variables have
definite, unchanging values throughout the system, the system is said to be in a
definite STATE. A quantity whose value depends only on the present state (not on
how the system reached it) is a STATE FUNCTION - pressure, volume, temperature
and internal energy are all state functions. Heat and work, by contrast, are NOT
state functions; they are path-dependent.

9.2 THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM AND THE ZEROTH LAW

Two systems are in THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM when, on being placed in thermal contact
(so that heat can flow between them), there is no net flow of heat and their
temperatures are equal. Everyday experience tells us that a hot body placed next
to a cold body eventually reaches a common temperature - they come to thermal
equilibrium.

The ZEROTH LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS states: if two systems A and B are each
separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then A and B are in
thermal equilibrium with each other. Although it sounds obvious, this law is what
makes the idea of TEMPERATURE meaningful. It tells us that there is a property -
temperature - which all bodies in mutual thermal equilibrium share, and that a
thermometer (system C) can be used to compare the temperatures of two bodies
without bringing them into direct contact. Temperature is thus defined as the
property that determines whether or not a body is in thermal equilibrium with its
neighbours.

9.3 INTERNAL ENERGY, HEAT AND WORK

The INTERNAL ENERGY U of a system is the total energy contained within it - the
sum of the kinetic energies of random molecular motion (translational,
rotational, vibrational) and the potential energies of intermolecular forces. It
does NOT include the bulk kinetic energy of the system as a whole or its
gravitational potential energy. Internal energy is a state function: it depends
only on the present state of the system. For an ideal gas the intermolecular
forces are negligible, so U depends only on temperature; U increases when T
increases.

HEAT (dQ) is energy that flows from one body to another BECAUSE of a temperature
difference between them. Heat is not something a body "contains" - it is energy
in transit. By convention, heat added TO the system is taken as positive.

WORK (dW) in thermodynamics usually means the mechanical work done by the system
on its surroundings as it expands (or the work done on the system when it is
compressed). Consider a gas enclosed by a piston of area A at pressure P. If the
piston moves out a small distance dx, the gas exerts a force P A and does work
 dW = P A dx = P dV,
where dV = A dx is the small increase in volume. For a finite change from volume
V1 to volume V2 the total work is the integral

 W = integral from V1 to V2 of P dV.

This integral is exactly the AREA under the curve on a P-V (pressure-volume)
diagram. Because the shape of that curve depends on HOW the change is carried
out, the work done is PATH-DEPENDENT: it is not a state function. Work done BY
the gas (expansion, dV positive) is positive; work done ON the gas (compression,
dV negative) is negative.

9.4 THE FIRST LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS

The first law is the principle of conservation of energy applied to thermal
systems. When a quantity of heat dQ is supplied to a system, part of it may raise
the internal energy of the system (by dU) and the rest may be used by the system
to do external work (dW). Hence

 dQ = dU + dW.

In words: the heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal
energy plus the work done by the system. Rearranged, dU = dQ - dW. The signs
follow the conventions above: dQ positive when heat is ADDED, dW positive when
work is done BY the system, and dU positive when the internal energy (and hence
temperature, for an ideal gas) rises.

Worked example. A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its
surroundings. Then dU = dQ - dW = 500 - 200 = 300 J; the internal energy rises by
300 J. If instead 500 J of heat were added while the gas was compressed with 200 J
of work done ON it (dW = -200 J), then dU = 500 - (-200) = 700 J.

9.5 SPECIFIC HEATS OF A GAS: Cp AND Cv

A gas has two important molar specific heats. Cv is the heat needed to raise the
temperature of one mole by one kelvin at CONSTANT VOLUME; Cp is the heat needed at
CONSTANT PRESSURE. At constant volume the gas does no work, so all the heat goes
into internal energy: dQ = dU = n Cv dT. At constant pressure the gas also
expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same temperature rise;
therefore Cp is always greater than Cv. Applying the first law to one mole heated
at constant pressure gives the important MAYER relation

 Cp - Cv = R.

The ratio gamma = Cp / Cv (the adiabatic index) is greater than 1; it is about
1.67 for a monatomic gas (like helium) and about 1.40 for a diatomic gas (like
air).

9.6 THERMODYNAMIC PROCESSES

A THERMODYNAMIC PROCESS is any change that takes a system from one state to
another. Four idealised processes are especially important.

(a) ISOTHERMAL process - carried out at CONSTANT TEMPERATURE. The system is kept
in contact with a large heat reservoir and the change is made very slowly. For an
ideal gas, since T is constant, P V = constant (Boyle's law); on a P-V diagram
this is a hyperbola (an isotherm). Because T (and hence U) does not change,
dU = 0, so by the first law dQ = dW - all the heat supplied is converted into work
(or all the work done on the gas is released as heat). The work done in an
isothermal expansion of n moles from V1 to V2 is

 W = n R T ln(V2 / V1) = 2.303 n R T log10(V2 / V1).

(b) ADIABATIC process - carried out with NO exchange of heat with the
surroundings (dQ = 0), either because the system is perfectly insulated or because
the change is very fast. From the first law, dQ = 0 gives dU = -dW: the work done
by the gas is done entirely at the expense of its internal energy, so an adiabatic
expansion COOLS the gas and an adiabatic compression HEATS it. For an ideal gas an
adiabatic change obeys

 P V^gamma = constant, and equivalently T V^(gamma - 1) = constant.

Because gamma > 1, an adiabatic curve on a P-V diagram is steeper than an
isotherm through the same point.

(c) ISOBARIC process - carried out at CONSTANT PRESSURE. The gas expands (or
contracts) while P stays fixed, so the work done is simply
 W = P (V2 - V1) = P dV = n R dT.
Heating a gas in a cylinder under a freely moving weighted piston is isobaric.

(d) ISOCHORIC (isovolumetric) process - carried out at CONSTANT VOLUME. Since
dV = 0, no work is done (W = 0), and the first law reduces to dQ = dU = n Cv dT.
All the heat supplied goes into internal energy, raising the temperature and
pressure. Heating a gas in a rigid closed vessel is isochoric.

9.7 REVERSIBLE AND IRREVERSIBLE PROCESSES

A REVERSIBLE process is an idealised process carried out so slowly (quasi-
statically) and without friction that at every instant the system is in
equilibrium, and it can be made to retrace its path exactly, returning both system
and surroundings to their original states. A slow isothermal expansion against an
almost-balanced pressure approaches reversibility. An IRREVERSIBLE process is one
that cannot be exactly reversed - the free expansion of a gas into vacuum, the
conduction of heat from a hot body to a cold one, and any process involving
friction are all irreversible. All REAL processes are irreversible; reversibility
is a useful limiting ideal.

9.8 THE SECOND LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS

The first law allows any energy-conserving change, but experience shows that many
such changes never happen: heat never flows on its own from a cold body to a hot
one, and no engine can turn ALL the heat it takes in into work. The SECOND LAW
captures this one-way character of nature. It has two equivalent classical
statements:

 KELVIN-PLANCK statement: it is impossible to construct an engine that, working
 in a cycle, takes heat from a single reservoir and converts it COMPLETELY into
 work, with no other effect. Some heat must always be rejected to a colder
 reservoir.

 CLAUSIUS statement: it is impossible for heat to flow, of its own accord, from a
 colder body to a hotter body without some external work being done. A
 refrigerator needs a compressor precisely for this reason.

The two statements look different but can be shown to be logically equivalent -
violating one would allow the other to be violated too.

9.9 HEAT ENGINE AND ITS EFFICIENCY

A HEAT ENGINE is a device that converts heat into mechanical work while working
in a repeating cycle. It has three essential parts: a SOURCE (hot reservoir) at
high temperature T1 from which the engine absorbs heat Q1; a WORKING SUBSTANCE
(such as steam or a gas) that undergoes the cycle; and a SINK (cold reservoir) at
lower temperature T2 to which the engine rejects heat Q2. Over one complete cycle
the working substance returns to its initial state, so its internal energy is
unchanged (dU = 0) and, by the first law, the net work output equals the net heat
input:

 W = Q1 - Q2.

The EFFICIENCY eta of the engine is the fraction of the absorbed heat that is
converted into useful work:

 eta = W / Q1 = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1 = 1 - Q2 / Q1.

Because Q2 can never be zero (Kelvin-Planck), eta is always less than 1 (less than
100 per cent). Efficiency is often quoted as a percentage.

Worked example. An engine absorbs 1000 J from the source and rejects 700 J to the
sink each cycle. Then W = 1000 - 700 = 300 J and eta = 300 / 1000 = 0.30 = 30 per
cent.

9.10 THE CARNOT ENGINE AND CARNOT CYCLE

In 1824 Sadi Carnot imagined the most efficient possible engine working between
two given temperatures - an idealised, fully REVERSIBLE engine using an ideal gas.
Its cycle, the CARNOT CYCLE, consists of four reversible steps:
 1. ISOTHERMAL EXPANSION at the source temperature T1: the gas absorbs heat Q1
    and does work.
 2. ADIABATIC EXPANSION: the gas continues to expand, doing work while cooling
    from T1 to T2 (no heat exchanged).
 3. ISOTHERMAL COMPRESSION at the sink temperature T2: the gas is compressed and
    rejects heat Q2.
 4. ADIABATIC COMPRESSION: the gas is compressed further, heating from T2 back to
    T1, returning to the starting state.

On a P-V diagram these four steps enclose a loop whose area is the net work done
per cycle. For the Carnot cycle it can be shown that Q1 / Q2 = T1 / T2, so the
efficiency depends ONLY on the two reservoir temperatures:

 eta(Carnot) = 1 - Q2 / Q1 = 1 - T2 / T1,

where T1 and T2 are measured on the absolute (kelvin) scale. This is CARNOT'S
THEOREM: no engine working between two temperatures can be more efficient than a
reversible (Carnot) engine operating between the same two temperatures, and all
reversible engines between the same two temperatures have the same efficiency. The
efficiency approaches 1 only if T2 approaches 0 K or T1 approaches infinity -
neither is attainable - so 100 per cent efficiency is impossible.

Worked example. A Carnot engine works between a source at 500 K and a sink at
300 K. Its efficiency is eta = 1 - 300/500 = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 = 40 per cent. If it
absorbs 1000 J per cycle, the work output is W = eta Q1 = 0.40 x 1000 = 400 J and
the heat rejected is Q2 = Q1 - W = 600 J.

9.11 REFRIGERATOR AND COEFFICIENT OF PERFORMANCE

A REFRIGERATOR (or heat pump) is a heat engine run in REVERSE. Using external work
W supplied by a compressor, it extracts heat Q2 from a cold body (the inside of
the fridge, at T2) and delivers heat Q1 = Q2 + W to a hotter body (the room, at
T1). Its performance is measured not by efficiency but by the COEFFICIENT OF
PERFORMANCE (COP), the ratio of the heat removed from the cold space to the work
supplied:

 COP = Q2 / W = Q2 / (Q1 - Q2).

For an ideal (reversible/Carnot) refrigerator, using Q1/Q2 = T1/T2,

 COP = T2 / (T1 - T2).

Unlike efficiency, the COP can be (and usually is) GREATER than 1: a good
refrigerator moves several joules of heat for each joule of work. The COP is
larger when T1 and T2 are close together, which is why a fridge works harder (and
less efficiently) on a hot day.

9.12 A BRIEF IDEA OF ENTROPY

The second law can be expressed quantitatively through a state function called
ENTROPY, usually written S. When a small quantity of heat dQ is added reversibly
to a system at absolute temperature T, its entropy changes by dS = dQ / T. Entropy
is a measure of the DISORDER or randomness of a system - a solid has lower entropy
than the liquid it melts into, which has lower entropy than the vapour. The second
law in its most general form states that in any spontaneous (natural) process the
TOTAL entropy of a system together with its surroundings can only INCREASE or, in
the limit of a reversible process, stay the same; it can never decrease. This
increase of entropy is what gives time its direction - it explains why heat flows
from hot to cold, why gases mix, and why no process can be perfectly efficient.

SUMMARY

- A thermodynamic system is the matter under study; the surroundings lie beyond
  its boundary. Systems are open, closed or isolated. Its state is fixed by state
  variables P, V, T, n (linked by P V = n R T for an ideal gas).
- Zeroth law: bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium
  with one another - this defines temperature.
- Internal energy U is the total molecular energy and is a state function; for an
  ideal gas it depends only on T. Heat and work are energy in transit and are
  path-dependent.
- Work in a volume change: W = integral P dV = area under the P-V curve.
- First law: dQ = dU + dW (energy conservation).
- Mayer relation: Cp - Cv = R; gamma = Cp/Cv.
- Isothermal (T constant): PV = const, dU = 0, dQ = dW, W = n R T ln(V2/V1).
  Adiabatic (dQ = 0): P V^gamma = const, dU = -dW. Isobaric (P constant): W = P dV.
  Isochoric (V constant): W = 0, dQ = dU.
- Second law: Kelvin-Planck (no engine converts heat wholly into work) and
  Clausius (heat does not flow cold-to-hot unaided) statements.
- Heat engine efficiency: eta = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1, always less than 1.
- Carnot engine (reversible) has the maximum efficiency eta = 1 - T2/T1 (kelvin).
- Refrigerator: COP = Q2/W = T2/(T1 - T2), can exceed 1.
- Entropy S is a measure of disorder; dS = dQ/T; the total entropy of an isolated
  system never decreases.

sections.heading: Systems, state variables and the Zeroth law
bullets: A thermodynamic system is the matter or region under study; the surroundings lie outside the boundary. Systems are open (exchange energy and matter), closed (energy only) or isolated (neither).
The state of a system is fixed by state variables P, V, T and n; for an ideal gas they obey P V = n R T. Quantities that depend only on the present state (P, V, T, U) are state functions.
Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when no net heat flows between them and their temperatures are equal.
Zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other. This defines temperature and justifies the thermometer.

sections.heading: Internal energy, heat, work and the first law
bullets: Internal energy U is the total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules; it is a state function and, for an ideal gas, depends only on temperature.
Heat dQ is energy flowing due to a temperature difference; work dW is mechanical energy transferred, e.g. by an expanding gas. Both are path-dependent (not state functions).
Work in a volume change is W = integral from V1 to V2 of P dV, equal to the area under the P-V curve. Expansion gives positive work.
First law: dQ = dU + dW - the heat supplied equals the rise in internal energy plus the work done by the system.
For a gas, Cp - Cv = R (Mayer relation) and gamma = Cp/Cv is greater than 1.

sections.heading: The four special processes
bullets: Isothermal (T constant): PV = constant, dU = 0, dQ = dW, and W = n R T ln(V2/V1).
Adiabatic (no heat exchange, dQ = 0): P V^gamma = constant, and dU = -dW so expansion cools the gas.
Isobaric (P constant): W = P (V2 - V1) = n R dT.
Isochoric (V constant): W = 0, so dQ = dU = n Cv dT; all heat raises the internal energy.
Real processes are irreversible; a reversible process is a slow, frictionless ideal that can retrace its path.

sections.heading: The second law and heat engines
bullets: Kelvin-Planck statement: no cyclic engine can convert heat from a single reservoir completely into work; some heat must be rejected.
Clausius statement: heat cannot flow of its own accord from a colder to a hotter body.
A heat engine absorbs Q1 from a hot source, does work W = Q1 - Q2, and rejects Q2 to a cold sink.
Efficiency eta = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1, always less than 1 (less than 100 per cent).

sections.heading: Carnot engine, refrigerator and entropy
bullets: The Carnot cycle is a reversible cycle of isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression and adiabatic compression.
Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T2/T1 (temperatures in kelvin) is the maximum possible between two given temperatures (Carnot's theorem).
A refrigerator is a reverse engine; its coefficient of performance is COP = Q2/W = T2/(T1 - T2), and can exceed 1.
Entropy S measures disorder; dS = dQ/T; the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases in a natural process.

key_takeaways: The state of a system is set by state variables (P, V, T, n); the Zeroth law makes temperature a meaningful, measurable property.
The first law dQ = dU + dW is simply conservation of energy: heat in = rise in internal energy + work done by the system.
Work done in a volume change equals the area under the P-V curve, W = integral P dV, and is path-dependent.
Each process has a signature: isothermal PV = const (W = nRT ln(V2/V1)); adiabatic P V^gamma = const (dQ = 0); isobaric W = P dV; isochoric W = 0.
The second law fixes the direction of change: heat cannot be fully converted to work, nor flow cold-to-hot without work.
A heat engine's efficiency is eta = 1 - Q2/Q1; the reversible Carnot engine sets the ceiling eta = 1 - T2/T1.
A refrigerator is an engine in reverse with COP = Q2/W = T2/(T1 - T2), and entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

A change at constant temperature; for an ideal gas PV = constant, dU = 0, and W = n R T ln(V2/V1).
A change with no heat exchange (dQ = 0); for an ideal gas P V^gamma = constant, so dU = -dW.
Kelvin-Planck: no engine converts heat wholly into work; Clausius: heat cannot flow unaided from cold to hot. It fixes the direction of change.

questions.question: Define a thermodynamic system, its surroundings and its boundary. Classify systems as open, closed and isolated with one example of each.
questions.answer:
A thermodynamic system is the definite quantity of matter or region of space chosen for study. The surroundings are everything outside it that can exchange energy or matter with it, and the boundary is the surface that separates the two.
- Open system: exchanges both energy and matter with the surroundings (e.g. water boiling in an open pan).
- Closed system: exchanges energy but not matter (e.g. gas sealed in a cylinder).
- Isolated system: exchanges neither energy nor matter (e.g. an idealised perfectly insulated flask).
questions.explanation: Definitions plus the three-way classification by what crosses the boundary.

questions.question: State the Zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain how it leads to the concept of temperature.
questions.answer: Zeroth law: if two systems A and B are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Its importance is that it shows there is a common property shared by all bodies in mutual thermal equilibrium - this property is called TEMPERATURE. It also justifies using a thermometer (the third system C) to compare temperatures of two bodies without bringing them into direct contact. Two bodies at the same temperature exchange no net heat.
questions.explanation: State the law and connect it to the definition of temperature and thermometry.

questions.question: State the first law of thermodynamics and explain the sign convention for dQ, dW and dU.
questions.answer: First law: dQ = dU + dW. The heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by the system on its surroundings; it is a statement of conservation of energy. Sign convention: dQ is positive when heat is ADDED to the system (negative when removed); dW is positive when work is done BY the system (expansion) and negative when work is done ON it (compression); dU is positive when the internal energy, and hence temperature of an ideal gas, increases.
questions.explanation: State dQ = dU + dW and give the three sign conventions.

questions.question: A gas absorbs 800 J of heat and, in the process, does 300 J of work on its surroundings. Find the change in its internal energy. What would dU be if the same heat were added while 300 J of work were done ON the gas?
questions.answer:
By the first law, dU = dQ - dW.
Case 1 (work done BY the gas, dW = +300 J): dU = 800 - 300 = +500 J. The internal energy increases by 500 J.
Case 2 (work done ON the gas, dW = -300 J): dU = 800 - (-300) = 800 + 300 = +1100 J. The internal energy increases by 1100 J.
questions.explanation: Apply dU = dQ - dW with the correct sign of the work for each case.

questions.question: Two moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally and reversibly at 300 K from a volume of 10 litre to 20 litre. Calculate the work done by the gas. (R = 8.314 J per mol per K; ln 2 = 0.693)
questions.answer:
For an isothermal process, W = n R T ln(V2/V1).
Here n = 2, T = 300 K, V2/V1 = 20/10 = 2.
W = 2 x 8.314 x 300 x ln 2 = 2 x 8.314 x 300 x 0.693.
2 x 8.314 = 16.628; 16.628 x 300 = 4988.4; 4988.4 x 0.693 = 3457 J (approximately).
So the gas does about 3.46 x 10^3 J = 3457 J of work. Since the process is isothermal, dU = 0 and the gas absorbs an equal amount of heat, dQ = W = 3457 J.
questions.explanation: Use W = nRT ln(V2/V1); note dQ = W because dU = 0 in an isothermal change.

questions.question: Distinguish between an isothermal and an adiabatic process. State the P-V relation obeyed by each for an ideal gas.
questions.answer:
Isothermal process: carried out at constant TEMPERATURE, in good thermal contact with a reservoir, very slowly. For an ideal gas P V = constant (Boyle's law). Since T is constant, dU = 0, so all heat supplied is converted to work (dQ = dW).
Adiabatic process: carried out with NO heat exchange (dQ = 0), the system being insulated or the change being very fast. For an ideal gas P V^gamma = constant (and T V^(gamma-1) = constant). Here the work done comes at the expense of internal energy (dU = -dW), so an adiabatic expansion cools the gas. Because gamma > 1, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isotherm on a P-V diagram.
questions.explanation: Contrast the constant quantity, the heat exchange and the P-V relation for each.

questions.question: Describe the working of a heat engine with a labelled account of its three essential parts, derive the expression for its efficiency, and explain why the efficiency can never be 100 per cent.
questions.answer:
A heat engine is a device that converts heat into mechanical work while operating in a repeating cycle. Its three essential parts are:
1. SOURCE (hot reservoir) at a high temperature T1, from which the engine absorbs heat Q1 in each cycle.
2. WORKING SUBSTANCE (such as steam or a gas), which undergoes the cyclic process and actually does the work.
3. SINK (cold reservoir) at a lower temperature T2, to which the engine rejects the unused heat Q2 each cycle.
Over one complete cycle the working substance returns to its initial state, so its internal energy is unchanged: dU = 0. By the first law, the net heat input equals the net work output:
 W = Q1 - Q2.
The efficiency is the fraction of the absorbed heat converted into useful work:
 eta = W/Q1 = (Q1 - Q2)/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1.
Efficiency cannot be 100 per cent because that would require Q2 = 0, i.e. all the absorbed heat converted into work with none rejected. The Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law forbids this: no cyclic engine can take heat from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work. Some heat must always be rejected to the sink, so Q2 > 0 and eta < 1.
questions.explanation: Parts, W = Q1 - Q2, eta = 1 - Q2/Q1, and the Kelvin-Planck reason for eta < 1.

questions.question: Describe the Carnot cycle through its four stages and state the expression for the efficiency of a Carnot engine. A Carnot engine works between 400 K and 300 K and absorbs 1200 J per cycle; find its efficiency, the work done and the heat rejected.
questions.answer:
The Carnot cycle is a reversible cycle with four stages, using an ideal gas between a source at T1 and a sink at T2:
1. Isothermal expansion at T1: the gas absorbs heat Q1 and does work.
2. Adiabatic expansion: the gas expands and cools from T1 to T2 with no heat exchange.
3. Isothermal compression at T2: the gas is compressed and rejects heat Q2.
4. Adiabatic compression: the gas is compressed and heats from T2 back to T1, completing the cycle.
The efficiency depends only on the two temperatures (in kelvin):
 eta = 1 - T2/T1.
Numerical part: T1 = 400 K, T2 = 300 K, Q1 = 1200 J.
 eta = 1 - 300/400 = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25 = 25 per cent.
 Work done W = eta x Q1 = 0.25 x 1200 = 300 J.
 Heat rejected Q2 = Q1 - W = 1200 - 300 = 900 J.
questions.explanation: Four reversible stages, eta = 1 - T2/T1, then substitute to get 25 per cent, W = 300 J, Q2 = 900 J.

questions.question: A refrigerator maintains its inside at 260 K while the room is at 300 K. Assuming ideal (Carnot) behaviour, find its coefficient of performance. If it extracts 520 J of heat from inside each cycle, how much work must the compressor supply?
questions.answer:
For an ideal (Carnot) refrigerator, COP = T2/(T1 - T2), with T2 the cold (inside) temperature and T1 the hot (room) temperature.
 COP = 260/(300 - 260) = 260/40 = 6.5.
The COP relates the heat removed to the work supplied: COP = Q2/W, so W = Q2/COP.
 W = 520/6.5 = 80 J.
Thus the compressor must supply 80 J of work to extract 520 J from inside (and it delivers Q1 = Q2 + W = 600 J to the room).
questions.explanation: COP = T2/(T1 - T2) = 6.5; then W = Q2/COP = 80 J.

questions.question: State the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements of the second law of thermodynamics, and explain what is meant by a reversible process.
questions.answer:
Kelvin-Planck statement: it is impossible to construct an engine that, working in a cycle, takes heat from a single reservoir and converts it completely into work with no other effect; some heat must be rejected to a colder body.
Clausius statement: it is impossible for heat to flow of its own accord from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being done.
A reversible process is an idealised process carried out so slowly (quasi-statically) and without friction that the system is in equilibrium at every stage and can be made to retrace its path exactly, restoring both system and surroundings to their original states. All real processes are irreversible; reversibility is a limiting ideal.
questions.explanation: Both statements plus the definition of a reversible (quasi-static, frictionless) process.

questions.question: Distinguish between an open, a closed and an isolated system with one example each.
questions.answer:
Open system: exchanges both energy and matter with the surroundings, e.g. water boiling in an open pan (heat and steam leave).
Closed system: exchanges energy but not matter, e.g. a fixed mass of gas sealed in a cylinder that can be heated.
Isolated system: exchanges neither energy nor matter, e.g. an idealised perfectly insulated closed flask.
questions.explanation: Classify by what crosses the boundary and give an example of each.

questions.question: What is meant by a state variable? Give three examples and say why heat is not one.
questions.answer: A state variable is a measurable property whose value depends only on the present state of the system, not on how that state was reached. Examples: pressure P, volume V and temperature T (also the amount n and internal energy U). Heat is NOT a state variable because it is energy in transit due to a temperature difference; the amount of heat exchanged depends on the path taken between two states, not just on the states themselves.
questions.explanation: State function depends only on the state; heat is path-dependent.

questions.question: State the Zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain its significance.
questions.answer: Zeroth law: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Significance: it establishes temperature as a fundamental, measurable property - all bodies in mutual thermal equilibrium have the same temperature. It also justifies the use of a thermometer, since the thermometer can play the role of the third system and be used to compare the temperatures of other bodies.
questions.explanation: State the law and connect it to temperature and thermometry.

questions.question: Explain why heat and work are called path functions while internal energy is a state function.
questions.answer: Internal energy U depends only on the current state of the system (for an ideal gas, only on its temperature); when a system goes from state A to state B, the change dU is the same no matter which path is taken. Heat and work, however, depend on HOW the change is carried out. For example, a gas can go from A to B by different paths on a P-V diagram, and the area under the curve (the work) and the heat exchanged differ between paths, even though dU is the same. Hence heat and work are path functions, and U is a state function.
questions.explanation: dU is path-independent; W (area under P-V) and Q depend on the path.

questions.question: Show that the work done by a gas expanding at constant pressure P from V1 to V2 is P(V2 - V1). A gas at 1.5 x 10^5 Pa expands from 2.0 L to 6.0 L; find the work.
questions.answer:
At constant pressure, W = integral from V1 to V2 of P dV = P integral dV = P(V2 - V1), since P is constant and comes out of the integral.
Numerical: P = 1.5 x 10^5 Pa, V1 = 2.0 L = 2.0 x 10^-3 m^3, V2 = 6.0 L = 6.0 x 10^-3 m^3.
W = 1.5 x 10^5 x (6.0 - 2.0) x 10^-3 = 1.5 x 10^5 x 4.0 x 10^-3 = 600 J.
questions.explanation: W = P dV at constant P; substitute to get 600 J.

questions.question: State the first law of thermodynamics and identify each term.
questions.answer: First law: dQ = dU + dW. Here dQ is the heat supplied to the system, dU is the increase in the internal energy of the system, and dW is the work done by the system on its surroundings. It states that the heat added to a system is used partly to raise its internal energy and partly to do external work - a statement of conservation of energy.
questions.explanation: dQ = dU + dW with each term defined.

questions.question: 500 J of heat is supplied to a gas which does 120 J of work. Find the change in internal energy. If the gas is monatomic, does its temperature rise or fall?
questions.answer: By the first law, dU = dQ - dW = 500 - 120 = +380 J. The internal energy increases by 380 J. Since for an ideal gas U increases with temperature, a positive dU means the TEMPERATURE RISES.
questions.explanation: dU = dQ - dW = 380 J; positive dU means temperature rises.

questions.question: Using the first law, prove that Cp is greater than Cv for an ideal gas.
questions.answer: Consider one mole heated by dT. At constant volume no work is done (W = 0), so dQ = dU = Cv dT; thus dU = Cv dT for any process of an ideal gas (since U depends only on T). At constant pressure the gas expands and does work dW = R dT (since P dV = R dT for one mole). The first law gives dQ = dU + dW, so Cp dT = Cv dT + R dT, i.e. Cp = Cv + R, hence Cp - Cv = R. Because R is positive, Cp is greater than Cv - the extra heat at constant pressure is needed to supply the work of expansion.
questions.explanation: At constant P extra heat R dT does the expansion work, so Cp = Cv + R.

questions.question: Name the four idealised thermodynamic processes and state the quantity kept constant in each.
questions.answer:
1. Isothermal process - temperature T is constant.
2. Adiabatic process - no heat is exchanged (dQ = 0).
3. Isobaric process - pressure P is constant.
4. Isochoric (isovolumetric) process - volume V is constant.
questions.explanation: List the four processes and their constant quantity.

questions.question: Why does a gas cool during an adiabatic expansion? Explain using the first law.
questions.answer: In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged, so dQ = 0. The first law dQ = dU + dW then gives dU = -dW. During an EXPANSION the gas does positive work on its surroundings (dW > 0), so dU is negative - the internal energy decreases. Since the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, a fall in U means a fall in temperature. Hence an adiabatic expansion cools the gas (and, conversely, an adiabatic compression heats it).
questions.explanation: dQ = 0 gives dU = -dW; expansion does work at the expense of U, so T falls.

questions.question: On a P-V diagram, both an isotherm and an adiabat pass through the same point. Which is steeper, and why?
questions.answer: The adiabat is steeper. For an isotherm PV = constant, differentiating gives a slope dP/dV = -P/V. For an adiabat P V^gamma = constant, the slope is dP/dV = -gamma P/V. Since gamma = Cp/Cv is greater than 1, the magnitude of the adiabatic slope (gamma P/V) is larger than that of the isothermal slope (P/V). Therefore, at the common point, the adiabatic curve falls more steeply than the isothermal curve.
questions.explanation: Slopes are -P/V (isotherm) and -gamma P/V (adiabat); gamma > 1 makes the adiabat steeper.

questions.question: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly at 400 K from V to 3V. Find the work done. (R = 8.314, ln 3 = 1.099)
questions.answer:
For an isothermal process, W = nRT ln(V2/V1). Here n = 1, T = 400 K, V2/V1 = 3.
W = 1 x 8.314 x 400 x ln 3 = 8.314 x 400 x 1.099.
8.314 x 400 = 3325.6; 3325.6 x 1.099 = 3655 J (approximately).
So the gas does about 3655 J of work. As dU = 0 for an isothermal change, the gas also absorbs 3655 J of heat.
questions.explanation: Apply W = nRT ln 3 = 3655 J; dQ equals W since dU = 0.

questions.question: Distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes with one example each.
questions.answer:
A reversible process is an idealised change carried out so slowly (quasi-statically) and without friction that the system is in equilibrium at every stage and can be made to retrace its path exactly, restoring both the system and the surroundings to their original states. Example: a very slow, frictionless isothermal expansion of a gas against an almost-balanced pressure.
An irreversible process cannot be exactly reversed; the system and surroundings cannot both be restored. Example: the free expansion of a gas into a vacuum, or conduction of heat from a hot to a cold body. All real processes are irreversible.
questions.explanation: Reversible = slow, frictionless, retraceable; irreversible = real, one-way.

questions.question: For a diatomic gas Cv = 5R/2. Find Cp and gamma. (R = 8.314)
questions.answer:
Using the Mayer relation, Cp = Cv + R = 5R/2 + R = 7R/2.
The adiabatic index gamma = Cp/Cv = (7R/2)/(5R/2) = 7/5 = 1.4.
Numerically, Cv = 5 x 8.314/2 = 20.8 J per mol per K and Cp = 7 x 8.314/2 = 29.1 J per mol per K.
questions.explanation: Cp = Cv + R = 7R/2; gamma = 7/5 = 1.4.

questions.answer:
Kelvin-Planck statement: it is impossible to construct an engine that, working in a cycle, takes heat from a single reservoir and converts it completely into work with no other effect; some heat must always be rejected.
Clausius statement: it is impossible for heat to flow of its own accord from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being done.
questions.explanation: Give both classical statements of the second law.

questions.question: What is entropy? State how the total entropy of an isolated system behaves in a natural process.
questions.answer: Entropy S is a state function that measures the degree of disorder or randomness of a system. When a small quantity of heat dQ is added reversibly to a system at absolute temperature T, its entropy changes by dS = dQ/T. In any natural (spontaneous, irreversible) process the TOTAL entropy of an isolated system - or of a system together with its surroundings - always increases; for a reversible process it stays the same. It can never decrease. This 'increase of entropy' gives natural processes their one-way direction.
questions.explanation: Entropy = disorder, dS = dQ/T; total entropy never decreases.

questions.question: Draw (describe) the energy flow in a heat engine and write the expression for its efficiency.
questions.answer:
A heat engine absorbs heat Q1 from a hot source at T1, converts part of it into useful work W, and rejects the remaining heat Q2 to a cold sink at T2. Since the working substance returns to its initial state each cycle (dU = 0), W = Q1 - Q2. The efficiency is the fraction of input heat turned into work:
 eta = W/Q1 = (Q1 - Q2)/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1.
questions.explanation: Q1 in, W out, Q2 rejected; eta = 1 - Q2/Q1.

questions.question: A heat engine absorbs 2000 J of heat and rejects 1500 J each cycle. Find the work done per cycle and the efficiency.
questions.answer:
Work done per cycle: W = Q1 - Q2 = 2000 - 1500 = 500 J.
Efficiency: eta = W/Q1 = 500/2000 = 0.25 = 25 per cent. (Equivalently, eta = 1 - Q2/Q1 = 1 - 1500/2000 = 0.25.)
questions.explanation: W = Q1 - Q2 = 500 J; eta = W/Q1 = 25 per cent.

questions.question: A Carnot engine operates between 500 K and 300 K and absorbs 1000 J per cycle. Find its efficiency, the work output and the heat rejected.
questions.answer:
Efficiency: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 300/500 = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 = 40 per cent.
Work output: W = eta x Q1 = 0.40 x 1000 = 400 J.
Heat rejected: Q2 = Q1 - W = 1000 - 400 = 600 J.
questions.explanation: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 40 per cent; W = 400 J; Q2 = 600 J.

questions.question: Explain why the efficiency of a Carnot engine cannot reach 100 per cent under practical conditions.
questions.answer: The Carnot efficiency is eta = 1 - T2/T1, with temperatures in kelvin. To make eta = 1 (100 per cent) we would need either T2 = 0 K (an absolute-zero sink) or T1 tending to infinity (an infinitely hot source). The third law of thermodynamics tells us that absolute zero cannot be reached, and no infinitely hot source is available, so T2/T1 can never be zero. Hence some heat is always rejected to the sink and eta is always less than 100 per cent. This is consistent with the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law.
questions.explanation: Would need T2 = 0 K or T1 = infinity, both impossible, so eta < 1.

questions.question: A domestic refrigerator maintains 4 C inside while the kitchen is at 30 C. Treating it as ideal, find its coefficient of performance. (Take 4 C = 277 K, 30 C = 303 K)
questions.answer:
For an ideal (Carnot) refrigerator, COP = T2/(T1 - T2), where T2 is the cold interior and T1 the warm kitchen.
 COP = 277/(303 - 277) = 277/26 = 10.7 (approximately).
So the ideal refrigerator would move about 10.7 J of heat from inside for every 1 J of work supplied. (A real fridge, being irreversible, has a smaller COP.)

questions.question: What is meant by the internal energy of a system? State two reasons why it is called a state function.
questions.answer: The internal energy U of a system is the total energy contained within it - the sum of the kinetic energies of the random molecular motion (translational, rotational, vibrational) and the potential energies of the intermolecular forces. It does not include the bulk kinetic energy of the system as a whole or its external potential energy. It is called a state function because (1) its value depends only on the present state of the system (for an ideal gas, only on the temperature), and (2) the change in U between two states is the same regardless of the path taken between them.
questions.explanation: U is total molecular energy; path-independent and depends only on state.

questions.question: Explain the concepts of thermodynamic system, surroundings and boundary. Classify systems and describe what state variables are, giving the equation of state of an ideal gas.
questions.answer:
A thermodynamic system is the definite quantity of matter or region of space chosen for study - for example the gas in a cylinder. The surroundings are everything outside the system that can exchange energy or matter with it, and the boundary is the real or imaginary surface separating the two.
Systems are classified by what can cross the boundary:
- Open system: both energy and matter can cross (water boiling in an open pan).
- Closed system: only energy can cross (gas sealed in a cylinder).
- Isolated system: nothing crosses (an idealised insulated flask).
The condition of a system is described by state variables (thermodynamic coordinates): pressure P, volume V, temperature T and amount n. When these have definite values throughout, the system is in a definite state. A quantity depending only on the state (P, V, T, U) is a state function; heat and work are not, being path-dependent. For a fixed amount of an ideal gas the state variables are linked by the equation of state P V = n R T, where R = 8.314 J per mol per K.
questions.explanation: Definitions, classification, state variables and PV = nRT.

questions.question: Derive the expression for work done by a gas during a volume change and explain why work is the area under the P-V curve. Use it to find the work when a gas at constant 2.0 x 10^5 Pa expands from 1.0 L to 4.0 L.
questions.answer:
Consider a gas enclosed by a piston of area A at pressure P. The gas exerts a force P A on the piston. If the piston moves out by a small distance dx, the work done by the gas is dW = (force) x (distance) = P A dx. But A dx = dV, the small increase in volume, so dW = P dV. For a finite change from V1 to V2 the total work is
 W = integral from V1 to V2 of P dV.
On a P-V diagram, P dV is the area of a thin vertical strip of height P and width dV; summing all such strips (the integral) gives the total area under the curve between V1 and V2. Hence the work done equals the area under the P-V curve, and because that area depends on the shape of the path, work is path-dependent.
Numerical: at constant pressure, W = P(V2 - V1) = 2.0 x 10^5 x (4.0 - 1.0) x 10^-3 = 2.0 x 10^5 x 3.0 x 10^-3 = 600 J.
questions.explanation: dW = P dV, integral = area under P-V; substitute to get 600 J.

questions.question: State the first law of thermodynamics and apply it to the isothermal and adiabatic processes, showing what each becomes. Then solve: a gas absorbs 700 J of heat and its internal energy rises by 450 J; find the work done.
questions.answer:
First law: dQ = dU + dW - the heat supplied equals the rise in internal energy plus the work done by the system (conservation of energy).
Isothermal process (T constant): for an ideal gas U depends only on T, so dU = 0; the first law becomes dQ = dW. All the heat supplied is converted into work (or all work done on the gas is released as heat).
Adiabatic process (dQ = 0): the first law becomes dU = -dW. The work done by the gas comes entirely from its internal energy, so an adiabatic expansion lowers U (cools the gas) and a compression raises it.
Numerical: dQ = 700 J, dU = 450 J. From the first law, dW = dQ - dU = 700 - 450 = 250 J. The gas does 250 J of work.
questions.explanation: dQ = dU + dW; isothermal -> dQ = dW, adiabatic -> dU = -dW; W = 250 J.

questions.question: Describe the four thermodynamic processes (isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric, isochoric), stating for each the constant quantity, the P-V-T relation, and the form the first law takes.
questions.answer:
1. Isothermal (constant T): PV = constant (Boyle's law). Since dU = 0, the first law becomes dQ = dW - all heat supplied is converted to work. Work W = nRT ln(V2/V1).
2. Adiabatic (no heat, dQ = 0): P V^gamma = constant and T V^(gamma-1) = constant. The first law becomes dU = -dW, so expansion cools the gas and compression heats it.
3. Isobaric (constant P): V/T = constant (Charles's law). Work W = P(V2 - V1) = nR dT, and dQ = dU + P dV = n Cp dT.
4. Isochoric (constant V): P/T = constant. Since dV = 0, W = 0 and the first law becomes dQ = dU = n Cv dT - all the heat raises the internal energy (and hence temperature and pressure).
questions.explanation: For each process: constant quantity, P-V-T relation, and the reduced first law.

questions.question: Two moles of an ideal gas are taken through an isothermal expansion at 350 K from 5.0 L to 15.0 L. (a) Find the work done. (b) Find the heat absorbed. (c) State the change in internal energy. (R = 8.314; ln 3 = 1.099)
questions.answer:
(a) For an isothermal process, W = nRT ln(V2/V1). Here n = 2, T = 350 K, V2/V1 = 15/5 = 3.
W = 2 x 8.314 x 350 x ln 3 = 2 x 8.314 x 350 x 1.099.
2 x 8.314 = 16.628; 16.628 x 350 = 5819.8; 5819.8 x 1.099 = 6396 J (approximately). So W = 6396 J.
(b) Since the process is isothermal, the internal energy of the ideal gas is unchanged, dU = 0. By the first law dQ = dU + dW = 0 + W = W. Therefore the heat absorbed dQ = 6396 J.
(c) The change in internal energy dU = 0, because the temperature is constant for an ideal gas.
questions.explanation: W = nRT ln 3 = 6396 J; dU = 0; dQ = W = 6396 J.

questions.question: State the two statements of the second law of thermodynamics, explain that they are equivalent, and discuss the meaning of entropy and the direction of natural processes.
questions.answer:
The second law of thermodynamics fixes the direction in which natural processes occur. It has two equivalent classical statements:
- Kelvin-Planck: it is impossible for an engine working in a cycle to take heat from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work with no other effect; some heat must be rejected to a colder body.
- Clausius: it is impossible for heat to flow of its own accord from a colder body to a hotter body without external work.
Equivalence: the two statements are logically equivalent. If a machine could violate the Kelvin-Planck statement (convert heat wholly into work), that work could be used to pump heat from cold to hot, violating Clausius; and vice versa. So a violation of one implies a violation of the other.
Entropy S is a state function measuring the disorder of a system, with dS = dQ/T for reversible heat exchange. The second law can be restated: the total entropy of an isolated system (or of a system plus its surroundings) can never decrease - it increases in every irreversible (natural) process and stays constant only for a reversible one. This increase of entropy is what gives natural processes their one-way direction in time.
questions.explanation: Both statements, their equivalence, and entropy as the direction-setting quantity.

questions.question: Explain the working of a heat engine and derive its efficiency. A heat engine absorbs 4000 J per cycle and rejects 3000 J. Find its efficiency and the work per cycle. If it runs 5 cycles per second, find its power output.
questions.answer:
A heat engine converts heat into work while operating in a repeating cycle. It absorbs heat Q1 from a hot source at T1, converts part into work W through the working substance, and rejects heat Q2 to a cold sink at T2. Over one complete cycle the working substance returns to its initial state, so dU = 0 and the first law gives W = Q1 - Q2. The efficiency is
 eta = W/Q1 = (Q1 - Q2)/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1.
Numerical: Q1 = 4000 J, Q2 = 3000 J.
 W = Q1 - Q2 = 4000 - 3000 = 1000 J per cycle.
 eta = W/Q1 = 1000/4000 = 0.25 = 25 per cent.
At 5 cycles per second, power = work per cycle x cycles per second = 1000 x 5 = 5000 W = 5 kW.
questions.explanation: W = Q1 - Q2 = 1000 J; eta = 25 per cent; power = 1000 x 5 = 5 kW.

questions.question: Describe the four stages of the Carnot cycle and state Carnot's theorem. A Carnot engine works between 600 K and 400 K, absorbing 1500 J per cycle. Find its efficiency, work output, heat rejected, and the coefficient of performance if the same device is run as a refrigerator between the same temperatures.
questions.answer:
The Carnot cycle has four reversible stages using an ideal gas between a source at T1 and a sink at T2:
1. Isothermal expansion at T1: gas absorbs Q1 and does work.
2. Adiabatic expansion: gas expands and cools from T1 to T2.
3. Isothermal compression at T2: gas is compressed and rejects Q2.
4. Adiabatic compression: gas is compressed and heats from T2 back to T1, completing the cycle.
Carnot's theorem: no engine working between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a reversible (Carnot) engine between the same two temperatures, and all reversible engines between them have the same efficiency.
Numerical (engine): T1 = 600 K, T2 = 400 K, Q1 = 1500 J.
 eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 400/600 = 1 - 0.667 = 0.333 = 33.3 per cent.
 W = eta Q1 = 0.333 x 1500 = 500 J.
 Q2 = Q1 - W = 1500 - 500 = 1000 J.
Run in reverse as a refrigerator between the same temperatures:
 COP = T2/(T1 - T2) = 400/(600 - 400) = 400/200 = 2.
questions.explanation: Four stages, Carnot's theorem; eta = 33.3 per cent, W = 500 J, Q2 = 1000 J, COP = 2.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A gas is enclosed in a metal cylinder fitted with a tightly sealed but movable piston. The cylinder can be heated from outside. No gas leaks out, but heat can pass through the metal walls.

(i) Is this an open, closed or isolated system? Justify.
(ii) Name the state variables that describe the gas.
(iii) Which equation links these variables for an ideal gas?
(iv) If the cylinder were replaced by a perfectly insulated, rigid, sealed one, what type of system would it be?
questions.answer:
(i) It is a CLOSED system: matter (the gas) cannot leave, but energy (heat) can cross the metal walls.
(ii) The state variables are pressure P, volume V, temperature T and the amount of gas n.
(iii) For an ideal gas they are linked by the equation of state P V = n R T, where R = 8.314 J per mol per K.
(iv) A perfectly insulated, rigid, sealed cylinder allows neither matter nor energy to cross the boundary, so it would be an ISOLATED system.
questions.explanation: Closed vs isolated depends on whether energy can cross; PV = nRT links the variables.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.0 x 10^5 Pa. Its volume increases from 2.0 x 10^-3 m^3 to 5.0 x 10^-3 m^3. During this process it absorbs 500 J of heat.

(i) Calculate the work done by the gas.
(ii) Using the first law, find the change in internal energy.
(iii) Did the temperature of the gas rise or fall? Why?
(iv) On a P-V diagram, what does the work correspond to?
questions.answer:
(i) At constant pressure, W = P(V2 - V1) = 1.0 x 10^5 x (5.0 - 2.0) x 10^-3 = 1.0 x 10^5 x 3.0 x 10^-3 = 300 J.
(ii) First law: dU = dQ - dW = 500 - 300 = +200 J.
(iii) The temperature ROSE, because dU is positive and, for an ideal gas, internal energy increases with temperature.
(iv) On a P-V diagram the work is the AREA under the P-V curve (here a rectangle of height P and width V2 - V1).
questions.explanation: W = P dV = 300 J; dU = dQ - dW = 200 J; positive dU means temperature rises.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In an experiment, 1200 J of heat is supplied to a gas. In one trial the gas is allowed to expand and does 400 J of work; in a second trial the same gas is held at constant volume.

(i) State the first law of thermodynamics.
(ii) Find the change in internal energy in the first trial.
(iii) Find the change in internal energy in the second trial.
(iv) Explain why the two answers differ.
questions.answer:
(i) First law: dQ = dU + dW - the heat supplied equals the increase in internal energy plus the work done by the system.
(ii) First trial: dW = 400 J, so dU = dQ - dW = 1200 - 400 = 800 J.
(iii) Second trial: at constant volume dW = 0, so dU = dQ = 1200 J.
(iv) The answers differ because in the first trial some of the supplied heat is spent doing external work (400 J), leaving less to raise the internal energy. At constant volume no work is done, so ALL the heat goes into internal energy.
questions.explanation: dU = dQ - dW; work reduces the rise in U in the expanding case.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A fixed mass of an ideal gas can be taken between two states either along an isothermal path or along an adiabatic path.

(i) What stays constant in the isothermal path, and what is the P-V relation?
(ii) What is zero in the adiabatic path, and what is the P-V relation?
(iii) In which process does the gas exchange heat with the surroundings?
(iv) Which curve is steeper on a P-V diagram, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) In the isothermal path the TEMPERATURE stays constant; the P-V relation is P V = constant (Boyle's law).
(ii) In the adiabatic path the HEAT exchanged is zero (dQ = 0); the P-V relation is P V^gamma = constant.
(iii) The gas exchanges heat with the surroundings in the ISOTHERMAL process (in the adiabatic process there is no heat exchange by definition).
(iv) The ADIABATIC curve is steeper, because its slope magnitude is gamma P/V compared with P/V for the isotherm, and gamma = Cp/Cv is greater than 1.
questions.explanation: Isothermal PV = const with heat exchange; adiabatic P V^gamma = const, dQ = 0, steeper.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

One mole of an ideal gas is expanded isothermally and reversibly at 300 K from a volume of 2.0 litre to 8.0 litre. (R = 8.314 J per mol per K; ln 4 = 1.386)

(i) Which formula gives the work done?
(ii) Calculate the work done by the gas.
(iii) How much heat is absorbed?
(iv) What is the change in internal energy?
questions.answer:
(i) For an isothermal process the work is W = n R T ln(V2/V1).
(ii) n = 1, T = 300 K, V2/V1 = 8/2 = 4. W = 1 x 8.314 x 300 x ln 4 = 8.314 x 300 x 1.386 = 2494.2 x 1.386 = 3457 J (approximately).
(iii) Since dU = 0 for an isothermal change of an ideal gas, the first law gives dQ = W = 3457 J. So 3457 J of heat is absorbed.
(iv) The change in internal energy is zero, dU = 0, because the temperature is constant.
questions.explanation: W = nRT ln 4 = 3457 J; dU = 0; dQ = W.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student claims to have built a ship engine that takes heat from the sea (a single large reservoir) and converts it entirely into work to drive the ship, rejecting no heat.

(i) Which law does this claim violate?
(ii) State that law in the form relevant to this claim.
(iii) Why must a real engine reject some heat?
(iv) Name the reservoir to which the heat must be rejected.
questions.answer:
(i) The claim violates the SECOND law of thermodynamics.
(ii) Kelvin-Planck statement: it is impossible for an engine working in a cycle to take heat from a single reservoir and convert it entirely into work with no other effect.
(iii) A real engine must reject some heat because complete conversion of heat into work in a cycle is forbidden by the second law; only part of the absorbed heat can become work, so Q2 > 0 always.
(iv) The heat must be rejected to a colder reservoir - the SINK (a body at a lower temperature than the source).
questions.explanation: This is a Kelvin-Planck violation; some heat must go to a cold sink.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A heat engine takes in 5000 J of heat from its source in each cycle and rejects 3500 J to its sink. The engine completes 4 cycles every second.

(i) Find the work done per cycle.
(ii) Find the efficiency of the engine.
(iii) Find the power output of the engine.
(iv) State one reason why the efficiency is less than 100 per cent.
questions.answer:
(i) Work per cycle: W = Q1 - Q2 = 5000 - 3500 = 1500 J.
(ii) Efficiency: eta = W/Q1 = 1500/5000 = 0.30 = 30 per cent.
(iii) Power = work per cycle x cycles per second = 1500 x 4 = 6000 W = 6 kW.
(iv) The efficiency is less than 100 per cent because the engine must reject some heat (Q2 = 3500 J) to the sink; by the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law, not all absorbed heat can be turned into work.
questions.explanation: W = Q1 - Q2 = 1500 J; eta = 30 per cent; power = 6 kW; second law forbids eta = 1.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A Carnot engine operates between a source at 800 K and a sink at 400 K. It absorbs 2000 J of heat from the source in each cycle.

(i) Calculate the efficiency of the engine.
(ii) Calculate the work done per cycle.
(iii) Calculate the heat rejected per cycle.
(iv) What would happen to the efficiency if the sink temperature were lowered?
questions.answer:
(i) Efficiency: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 400/800 = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5 = 50 per cent.
(ii) Work per cycle: W = eta x Q1 = 0.5 x 2000 = 1000 J.
(iii) Heat rejected: Q2 = Q1 - W = 2000 - 1000 = 1000 J.
(iv) Lowering the sink temperature T2 increases the ratio (T1 - T2)/T1, so the efficiency eta = 1 - T2/T1 would INCREASE (approaching 100 per cent only if T2 approached 0 K, which is unattainable).
questions.explanation: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 50 per cent; W = 1000 J; Q2 = 1000 J; lower T2 raises eta.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A refrigerator keeps its freezer at 250 K while rejecting heat to a kitchen at 300 K. In each cycle its compressor does 100 J of work, and the appliance is close to ideal (Carnot) behaviour.

(i) Write the expression for the coefficient of performance of an ideal refrigerator.
(ii) Calculate the COP for this refrigerator.
(iii) How much heat is extracted from the freezer per cycle?
(iv) How much heat is delivered to the kitchen per cycle?
questions.answer:
(i) For an ideal (Carnot) refrigerator, COP = T2/(T1 - T2), where T2 is the cold freezer and T1 the warm kitchen.
(ii) COP = 250/(300 - 250) = 250/50 = 5.
(iii) COP = Q2/W, so the heat extracted Q2 = COP x W = 5 x 100 = 500 J per cycle.
(iv) Heat delivered to the kitchen Q1 = Q2 + W = 500 + 100 = 600 J per cycle.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When a hot cup of coffee is left on a table, it cools until it reaches room temperature. The reverse - the coffee spontaneously growing hotter by drawing heat from the cooler room - is never observed, even though it would not violate the first law.

(i) Why does the reverse process not violate the first law?
(ii) Which law forbids the reverse process?
(iii) State the relevant statement of that law.
(iv) Explain the direction of the process in terms of entropy.
questions.answer:
(i) The reverse process does not violate the first law because energy would still be conserved - the heat gained by the coffee would simply equal the heat lost by the room. The first law says nothing about the DIRECTION of energy flow.
(ii) The SECOND law of thermodynamics forbids the reverse process.
(iii) Clausius statement: heat cannot flow of its own accord from a colder body (the room) to a hotter body (the coffee) without external work.
(iv) The natural process (coffee cooling) increases the total entropy of the coffee-plus-room system, because heat flowing from hot to cold raises total disorder. The reverse would DECREASE total entropy, which the second law forbids for a spontaneous process. So entropy increase sets the observed direction.
questions.explanation: First law allows it; second law (Clausius) and increase of entropy forbid the reverse.
